text: Trained 300,000+ demand-forecasting models across a CPG portfolio to optimize trade promotions — delivering ~$2.4M in client savings, on pipelines processing 100M+ rows a day.

title: Saving a CPG client $2.4M on trade promotions
text:
The problem
A CPG client planned trade promotions off forecasts that were too coarse to trust at the SKU × store level, so promo spend was routinely mis-sized. The business needed accurate, per-series demand forecasts across a very large portfolio — and needed them to refresh fast enough to plan against. [[TODO: one sentence on the specific decision the forecast fed — promo depth? volume commitment?]]

title: Saving a CPG client $2.4M on trade promotions
text:
The finding


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
t = np.arange(60)
base = 100 + 18 * np.sin(t / 6)
actual = base + rng.normal(0, 5, 60)
actual[20:24] += 40          # a promotion spike
fc = base.copy(); fc[20:24] += 34
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
ax.fill_between(t, fc - 10, fc + 10, color="#2563eb", alpha=0.12, label="80% interval")
ax.plot(t, actual, color="#8a909a", lw=1.6, label="actual")
ax.plot(t, fc, color="#2563eb", lw=2.6, label="forecast")
ax.axvspan(20, 23, color="#fde68a", alpha=0.4, label="promotion")
ax.set_xlabel("week"); ax.set_ylabel("units")
ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=2)
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color("#d5d5df"); ax.spines["bottom"].set_color("#d5d5df")
ax.grid(axis="y", color="#eef0f4", lw=1)
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("hero.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor="white")
plt.show()








Figure 1: Per-series forecast vs. actuals with prediction interval. Replace the synthetic series with a representative real backtest window.





Getting the promotion weeks right (the yellow band) is where the savings came from — that’s where a generic forecast fails and money is left on the table.

title: Saving a CPG client $2.4M on trade promotions
text:
Decisions and tradeoffs
Training a separate model per series (300k+ of them) was a deliberate choice over one global model: it captured per-SKU seasonality and promo response that a pooled model washed out, at the cost of a much heavier training and orchestration burden. I ran this on a distributed stack (PySpark / Databricks / Dask) so the whole portfolio could retrain on 100M+ rows a day. title: Production RAG + NL2SQL over live business data

The problem
Stakeholders needed answers from data they couldn’t query themselves, and hand-written reports couldn’t keep up. The system had to translate natural-language questions into correct SQL and ground its answers in retrieved context — reliably enough to trust in front of the business. I also co-built a time-series anomaly detection accelerator with automated root-cause analysis, a trade-promotion optimization tool for a UK client, and prototyped an LLM + RAG marketing assistant that took 2nd place in Tiger Analytics’ internal hackathon.
Earlier roles: Data Scientist & Developer at vCreaTek (real-estate decision support systems, API gateway productionization), a Software Engineer Apprenticeship at Persistent Systems (led an 8-person team building a COVID-19 pedestrian-detection pipeline in one month), and an AI internship at IoTIoT.in (face-recognition pipeline, MTCNN + FaceNet). I hold a B.E. in Computer Science from Dr. D. Y. Patil Institute of Technology (SPPU, Pune), First Class with Distinction.
Tools I reach for: Python, SQL, PySpark, Databricks, Spark, Dask, scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow, FastAPI, Streamlit, RAG/vector stores, and OpenAI/Hugging Face for LLM work.

title: Cutting anomaly false positives 35% on multivariate time series
text: Reduced anomaly-detection false positives by 35% on multivariate time-series signals — cutting alert fatigue without missing the real incidents.

title: Cutting anomaly false positives 35% on multivariate time series
text:
The problem
The existing detector fired too often, and every false alarm cost an analyst’s time and eroded trust in the system. The goal was to keep recall on genuine anomalies while sharply cutting the false-positive rate on correlated, multivariate signals. [[TODO: one sentence on what the signals were and what a missed anomaly cost the business.]]

title: Cutting anomaly false positives 35% on multivariate time series
text:
The finding


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
t = np.arange(200)
sig = np.sin(t / 9) + 0.4 * np.sin(t / 3) + rng.normal(0, 0.15, 200)
anom = np.array([40, 96, 150, 178])
sig[anom] += np.array([1.8, -1.6, 2.0, -1.7])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
ax.plot(t, sig, color="#8a909a", lw=1.3)
ax.scatter(anom, sig[anom], color="#dc2626", s=42, zorder=3,
           edgecolors="white", lw=0.8, label="detected anomaly")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.set_xlabel("time"); ax.set_ylabel("signal")
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color("#d5d5df"); ax.spines["bottom"].set_color("#d5d5df")
ax.grid(axis="y", color="#eef0f4", lw=1)
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("hero.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor="white")
plt.show()








Figure 1: Multivariate signal with flagged anomalies. Red = detected; the tightened model stops flagging the normal correlated wobble.





The win was modeling the correlation between signals, so normal joint movement stopped tripping single-variable thresholds.

title: Cutting anomaly false positives 35% on multivariate time series
text:
Decisions and tradeoffs
I moved from per-signal thresholding toward a multivariate approach that models the joint distribution, so a change is only anomalous relative to how the signals usually move together. [[TODO: name the method — PyOD ensemble? a reconstruction model like InterFusion? — and why over the simpler baseline.]] I used SHAP to make each alert explainable, which mattered as much as the score itself for analyst trust.
